title: FalcHub — Edge-to-Cloud File Sync Sidecar
one_liner: Designed and built FalcHub, a production edge sidecar (Python) that reliably syncs GB-scale daily file volume from field devices to AWS S3 over unreliable networks — using a concurrent multi-process pipeline, certificate-based IoT auth, and crash-safe atomic state.
problem: Unattended edge devices in industrial environments produce GB-scale file volume every day and must upload it to the cloud continuously for months — over decent-but-unreliable LAN/WiFi links that drop frequently — surviving crashes, power loss, and outages without ever losing or double-uploading data, and without storing any static cloud credentials on the device.
solution: Built a fork-based supervisor process that isolates three worker processes (file discovery, upload, and cleanup) communicating only through a shared SQLite ledger with atomic, crash-safe state transitions. High per-device file volume is absorbed by a concurrent pipeline that keeps scanning, uploading, and retention from blocking each other; files upload to AWS S3 using short-lived credentials obtained via AWS IoT X.509 certificate authentication, are confirmed with a backend API, and are deleted only after a retention-gated, confirmed sync.
impact: GB-scale files synced per device, every day
3 isolated worker processes for concurrent, non-blocking throughput
Zero data loss across crashes and unreliable-network drops
0 static AWS keys — short-lived IoT credentials only
technical_details: Concurrency via process isolation: independent Walker/Uploader/Cleaner workers so high per-device file volume never blocks scanning, upload, or retention — sustaining throughput on constrained edge hardware
Resilient to unreliable LAN/WiFi: bounded retries with a transport-vs-permanent failure classifier and a watchdog that reclaims stalled uploads, so files still reach S3 despite frequent link drops
Efficient at scale: an atomic compare-and-swap claim ensures workers never contend or re-upload a file, and per-process credential caching avoids repeated STS round-trips
Fork-safe supervisor (SystemOrchestrator) with restart-storm throttling and a staged shutdown ladder for months of unattended operation
Zero-ambient-credentials model: every S3 client requires explicit IoT-issued temporary credentials via an X.509 → role-alias → STS exchange

Two-stage Docker build compiling a patched SQLite (SHA3-256 pinned) to fix a WAL-checkpoint bug, enforced by a boot-time and build-time safety gate; Jenkins CI/CD with cosign signing + SPDX SBOM attestation to Harbor/ECR
suggested_visuals: File lifecycle state machine (pending → uploading → synced/failed)
Zero-credential IoT → STS credential exchange flow
recruiter_angle: Demonstrates high-volume, constrained-network edge throughput plus production security and supply-chain depth — concurrent crash-safe process design and end-to-end signed/attested delivery, owned solo.

title: VisitorLog — Multi-Site Visitor Management Platform
one_liner: Architected and built VisitorLog end to end — a multi-site platform serving many kiosks and concurrent approvers with low-latency check-in, signed QR badge credentials, and an efficient, horizontally scalable zero-trust FastAPI + Next.js + PostgreSQL stack.
problem: A multi-site organization needed to replace manual, ad-hoc visitor tracking with a governed workflow that serves many kiosks and tens of concurrent approvers across sites — routing each of hundreds of daily visits through the correct security approval based on classification, protecting sensitive PII, and producing a complete, auditable record of every visit and system access, all without sacrificing kiosk responsiveness.
solution: Designed a horizontally scalable 3-tier system (Cloudflare Access → Next.js BFF → FastAPI API → PostgreSQL) with a stateless API and pooled database connections to serve concurrent kiosks and approvers efficiently. It routes visit requests to the right approver by security classification, collects and encrypts only the PII each classification requires, and issues signed, site-scoped QR credentials that unattended kiosks verify in-process for sub-second check-in, badge printing, and checkout — all behind zero-trust, per-application edge authentication.
impact: 73 API endpoints across 17 routers
Multi-site, many-kiosk deployment
Sub-second kiosk check-in and QR validation
193 automated tests running in CI
technical_details: Built for horizontal scale: a stateless FastAPI service with pooled PostgreSQL connections serves many kiosks and tens of concurrent approvers across sites without per-request connection churn
Low-latency kiosk path: signed QR (VLQ1) credentials are verified cryptographically in-process — no round-trip to a token store — keeping check-in/checkout sub-second under load
Rate-limited (slowapi) public kiosk surface stays responsive and abuse-resistant while unauthenticated
Parallel Dockerized CI stages (backend pytest + frontend Vitest/tsc/ESLint) keep the pipeline fast as the codebase grows
Zero-trust, per-area JWT audience scoping so tokens from one Cloudflare Access surface cannot be replayed on another
Field-level PII encryption at rest gated by visit classification; 42-model schema carried through 18 zero-downtime Alembic migrations
suggested_visuals: 3-tier architecture: Cloudflare Access → Next.js BFF → FastAPI → PostgreSQL
Signed QR credential issuance + kiosk check-in sequence
recruiter_angle: Strong end-to-end full-stack case study — a horizontally scalable multi-site platform with low-latency kiosk UX and zero-trust security (signed credentials, encrypted PII, per-area token scoping), architected and shipped solo to v1.0.0.

title: Coordination Substrate — One Decision, Three Production Systems
one_liner: Inherited five production systems, three of them pinned to a single worker for the same underlying reason — designed one Postgres-native coordination substrate, applied it across all three, and deliberately did not apply it to the fourth.
problem: Three production systems could not run more than one worker, each for what looked locally like a separate reason: in-process singleton daemons (crash recovery, cron scheduling, budget reconciliation) sitting behind a boot guard that actively refused multi-worker startup; an in-memory task queue that lost every in-flight batch on a routine deploy; and a process-local event hub that fanned out only to subscribers connected to that same process. Treated separately they were three scaling projects needing three sets of new infrastructure, and none of the three had a baseline measurement, so none could be changed safely.
solution: Audited every piece of in-process state across the systems and classified it five ways — singleton jobs, fan-out, shared ephemeral state, durable work, and benign duplication that needed no coordination at all — which established that one substrate covered the real cases and that several apparent problems needed nothing done to them. Chose Postgres-native primitives over Redis and managed queues because all three systems already ran Postgres and one ships to an on-premise industrial box with no on-site operator, where an additional service is a permanent operational cost rather than a one-time setup. Built leader election, durable queueing, and fan-out on that substrate, proved each independently, then removed the single-worker guards and re-ran the capacity benchmarks unchanged.
impact: 3 production systems unpinned from a single worker
100% in-flight task survival across restart, up from 0%
10 architecture decision records authored with rejected alternatives
5 production systems audited and state-classified
technical_details: Leader election on Postgres advisory locks held on a dedicated connection outside the pool — a pooled connection returned to the pool silently releases the lock and lets two workers run the same scheduler, so the holder runs a supervision loop that re-acquires after network blips while non-holders retry on a bounded cadence for predictable failover

Durable work queue on a jobs table consumed with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so workers never block each other, with attempt-counted exponential backoff persisted in the row rather than in memory, and a reaper that reclaims work from a worker that died mid-task

Fan-out via LISTEN/NOTIFY on a per-tenant channel, viable specifically because the frontend already treats an event as a cache-invalidation hint rather than as data — so payloads stay a bare identifier and a missed notification degrades to slightly stale data instead of lost data

A deliberate boundary on the pattern: token-level streaming is high-frequency and stateful, so it uses sticky routing that pins a turn to its executing worker and scales across threads, rather than being forced through a notification channel that is the wrong instrument for it

Shared ephemeral state resolved by measurement rather than reflex — process-local rate-limit counters meant N workers enforced N times the configured limit, but measured traffic was low enough that a Postgres counter table with periodic cleanup was sufficient, and the metrics registry was deliberately left per-worker and scraped separately since multi-process aggregation modes are more fragile than the standard answer

Single-worker guards removed only after each mechanism was independently proven, then benchmarks re-run unchanged in the same harness on the same data — including behaviour under worker failure, with failover tested by killing processes rather than mocking them
suggested_visuals: In-process state classification: five classes across three systems, including what needed nothing
Advisory-lock leader election with failover on holder death
Job lifecycle under SKIP LOCKED: claim → process → terminal, with reaper reclaim
Substrate decision matrix: Postgres-native vs. Redis vs. managed, against the on-premise constraint
recruiter_angle: Senior-level systems judgment rather than feature delivery — one architectural decision amortized across three production systems, an explicit and defended boundary where the pattern did not fit, and changes gated on measurement rather than assumption.

title: Making Two LLM Systems Measurable — Then Cheaper
one_liner: Two production LLM systems had precise cost observability and no quality observability at all — built evaluation harnesses for both, then used them to gate cost reductions that would otherwise have silently degraded the product.
problem: One platform could report exactly what an agent run cost and nothing whatsoever about whether the output was any good, so no prompt or model change could be validated except by inspection. The other ranked candidates using scoring weights that were unmeasured guesses, and its largest available cost saving — cascading so the expensive model only ever sees a shortlist — would have handed the cheap prefilter authority over which candidates the strong model was allowed to see. That is precisely the failure the hybrid design existed to prevent, and nothing in either system could tell you whether shipping it would be free or actively harmful.
solution: Split evaluation into two kinds of check that need different treatment: deterministic contract conformance, which has unambiguous answers and can gate CI hard, and rubric-scored quality, which is noisy and gates on a threshold plus human sign-off. Built the ranking evaluation set out of ground truth the organization already had and had never used — its own hiring outcomes, which are a labelled relevance set — and used it to replace guessed scoring weights with measured ones. Only then ran the cost work, with every optimization recording before and after in the same harness and stating the quality tradeoff alongside the saving.
impact: 2 LLM systems moved from cost-only to quality observability
5 deterministic contract checks gating every prompt and model-route change
4 ranking metrics measured against real hiring outcomes
1 unbounded prompt-growth defect found and bounded
technical_details: Deterministic contract checks — schema validity, tool-call allowlist, secret-access contract, budget cap, and terminal-state reachability — block a merge outright, while quality regression beyond a threshold requires explicit human sign-off instead, because a hard gate on a noisy metric only trains people to bypass the gate

Ranking evaluation set built from hiring outcomes as a labelled relevance set, deliberately excluding rankings produced before the ranker was replaced — those are invalid, and building on them would have silently invalidated every downstream cost conclusion in a way that stays invisible until much later

Recall@k chosen as the primary metric over precision, because a screening tool's catastrophic failure is a strong candidate never appearing in the shortlist at all — which nobody ever discovers — whereas an over-ranked mediocre candidate is caught by a human in the interview

Cascade ranking gated on the measured recall@K of the cheap first pass rather than on the obvious call-count saving, with K set above the operator's shortlist size so the marginal calls buy protection against prefilter error, and a two-tier model cascade held in reserve for the case where lexical recall proved too low to prefilter on safely

Escalation economics computed explicitly before shipping: with a cheap model at cost c, a strong model at s, and cheap-model success rate p, default-cheap-escalate-on-failure only wins when p > c/s — since a failed cheap call followed by a strong call costs strictly more than the strong call alone

Found and bounded an unbounded prompt-growth defect: approved data-tier proposals were appended to a living-context store injected into every system prompt, with no size cap and no compaction, so each approval permanently raised cost and latency for every future turn while progressively diluting the instructions that mattered — fixed with a cap plus compaction, and by surfacing context size in the approval interface so the cost is visible to the person creating it

Prompt prefixes restructured so stable content (system prompts, contract descriptions, skill definitions) precedes the variable portion, which is what makes a prefix eligible for provider-side caching at all — applies to every call with no quality tradeoff
suggested_visuals: Cascade ranking: N candidates → cheap pass → top K → strong model, with the recall@K gate
Evaluation split: deterministic contract checks (hard CI gate) vs. rubric quality checks (threshold + sign-off)
Escalation break-even: where p > c/s makes default-cheap actually cheaper
Living-context growth: unbounded append-only vs. capped with compaction
recruiter_angle: Directly relevant to GenAI and applied-ML roles — builds the quality measurement layer most LLM systems lack, then uses it to make cost decisions with the tradeoff quantified rather than assumed.

title: BeltIQ — Taking an Edge AI Safety Product From Zero to One
one_liner: Owned BeltIQ as product manager from a site observation to a deployed product — turning an open-ended safety problem into a sequenced roadmap, a hardware supply chain, and a market-entry story a buyer could evaluate.
problem: "Make the conveyor belt safer" is a mandate, not a specification. Belt failures at a mine site are expensive and dangerous, but the operators experiencing them described symptoms — a spill nobody caught, a misalignment found on the next walk-around — not requirements. There was no product to sell, no reference deployment to point at, and no obvious first slice: the problem could plausibly start at any of a dozen failure modes, each implying different cameras, different mounting, different compute, and a different buyer conversation. Compounding it, the work spanned ML, software, hardware, and field deployment teams with no shared plan between them, and the hardware those teams depended on had procurement lead times measured in weeks — long enough that a scoping mistake made in month one would not surface as a schedule problem until month three.
solution: Started with discovery rather than architecture: sat with site operators and decision-makers to separate what actually hurt from what was merely annoying, and used that to pick a first failure mode narrow enough to build against and severe enough to justify a purchase. Broke the resulting problem into thin vertical slices — each one a working end-to-end path from camera to alert rather than a horizontal layer — so every increment produced something a client could watch running on their own site instead of deferring all value to a single launch. Laid the slices onto a technical roadmap with an explicit execution plan, then ran hardware selection and vendor procurement against that sequence so lead times were absorbed by the plan rather than discovered by it. Built the pitch deck and product narrative in parallel with the build, which forced the positioning and the market-entry strategy to be decided while they could still change what got built, not after.
impact: Zero to one — from site observation to a deployed product on a live mine site
One roadmap shared across ML, software, hardware, and field-deployment teams
Market-entry strategy and pitch narrative defined before first client demo
Hardware selection and procurement sequenced against delivery milestones
technical_details: Requirements gathered from operators in the language of their workflow — what they walk past, what they check, what they escalate — then translated into detection targets, latency tolerances, and false-alarm budgets engineering could actually design against; an alert nobody trusts is worse than no alert, so the acceptable false-positive rate was treated as a product requirement rather than a model metric

Scope decomposed into thin vertical slices rather than horizontal layers, so the first shippable increment ran the full path — camera, on-device inference, alert, operator response — on real site hardware, which surfaced mounting, lighting, network, and power problems while they were still cheap to fix

Roadmap sequenced so that the longest-lead-time item in each phase started first, with hardware procurement, site-access scheduling, and model development running as parallel tracks with named join points instead of a serial chain where any slip propagated to the whole plan

Vendor management run as an evaluated selection rather than a purchase order: edge compute, cameras, and installation hardware assessed against the real deployment constraint — an industrial box on a remote site with no on-site operator, where a component failure costs a truck roll — with a second source identified for the parts on the critical path

Feature planning driven by what changed an operator's decision, not by what was technically interesting: capabilities that produced information nobody would act on were explicitly deferred, and that deferral was written down with its reasoning so it did not get relitigated every planning cycle

Client and executive communication run on a cadence that surfaced tradeoffs and scope changes while they were still decisions — a shifted date raised in advance with options attached lands as a plan, and the same date raised late lands as an escalation

Sales pitch deck built around the operational outcome rather than the model architecture, framing edge AI capability in terms a buyer evaluates — incidents caught, manual monitoring hours displaced, and what the system costs to run unattended on their site
suggested_visuals: Discovery to specification: operator symptoms → failure modes → detection targets with false-alarm budgets
Thin vertical slices vs. horizontal layers: what each increment put in front of the client
Roadmap with parallel tracks — procurement, site access, model development — and their join points
Vendor evaluation matrix against the unattended-remote-site constraint, with critical-path second sourcing
recruiter_angle: Product ownership backed by the ability to build the thing — discovery, roadmap, procurement, and go-to-market for a physical-world AI product, with the engineering judgment to know which slice is actually shippable first. Relevant to AI product management, founding-engineer, and forward-deployed roles where the same person has to talk to the client and scope the build.
